```{r}
#| label: setup

library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
data(diamonds)
library(ggimage)
library(ggrepel)
library(patchwork)
```

# Diamonds Table of Statistics

In order to examine the dimensions of diamonds across different tiers of
quality, descriptive statistics were calculated for their length, width, and
depth, grouped by the quality of their cut. @tbl-length shows us that Ideal cut
diamonds are the smallest in terms of length across most of the descriptive
statistics, while Fair cut diamonds are the largest and the least variable.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-length
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive Statistics of Diamond Length (mm) by Cut Quality"
#| tbl-pos: H

# Step 3: Make new data frame and select only needed data ----
diamondsLength <- diamonds |>
  select(cut, x)|>
  filter(x != 0) |>
  # Step 4: group by cut ----
group_by(cut) |>
  ## Step 5: create descriptive statistics ----
summarize(
  Count = n(),
  Minimum = min(x),
  Quintile1 = quantile(x, probs = 0.20),
  Quintile2 = quantile(x, probs = 0.40),
  Median = median(x),
  Quintile3 = quantile(x, probs = 0.60),
  Quintile4 = quantile(x, probs = 0.80),
  Maximum = max(x),
  Mean = mean(x),
  StandardDeviation = sd(x),
  .groups = "drop"
)
## Step 6: Create clean table ----
diamondsLength |>
  kable(
    digits = 2,
    col.names = c("Cut Quality", "Freq.", "Min", "20%-tile", "40%-tile",
                  "Median", "60%-tile", "80%-tile", "Max", "SAM", "SASD"),
    format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
    align = "lcccccccccc",
    format = "latex"
  ) |>
  kable_classic(font_size = 10, lightable_options = "striped") |>
    add_footnote(
    label = c("Length was measured in milimeters."),
    notation = "none",
    threeparttable = TRUE) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "scale_down")
```

@tbl-width summarizes the distribution of diamond width (`y`) across cut
categories, displaying that Fair cut diamonds are the widest and most variable
cut of diamond according to most descriptive statistics, and that Ideal cut
diamonds are of the smallest width and least variability. However, both the
Premium cut and Ideal Cut diamonds have very large outlier maximums, multiple
times larger than the maximums of the other three cuts.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-width
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive Statistics of Diamond Width (mm) by Cut Quality"
#| tbl-pos: H

# Step 3: Make new data frame and select only needed data ----
diamondsWidth <- diamonds |>
  select(cut, y) |>
    filter(y != 0) |>
  # Step 4: group by cut ----
group_by(cut) |>
  ## Step 5: create descriptive statistics ----
summarize(
  Count = n(),
  Minimum = min(y),
  Quintile1 = quantile(y, probs = 0.20),
  Quintile2 = quantile(y, probs = 0.40),
  Median = median(y),
  Quintile3 = quantile(y, probs = 0.60),
  Quintile4 = quantile(y, probs = 0.80),
  Maximum = max(y),
  Mean = mean(y),
  StandardDeviation = sd(y),
  .groups = "drop"
)
## Step 6: Create clean table ----
diamondsWidth |>
  kable(
    digits = 2,
    col.names = c("Cut Quality", "Freq.", "Min", "20%-tile", "40%-tile",
                  "Median", "60%-tile", "80%-tile", "Max", "SAM", "SASD"),
    format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
    align = "lcccccccccc",
    format = "latex"
  ) |>
  kable_classic(font_size = 10, lightable_options = "striped") |>
    add_footnote(
    label = c("Width was measured in milimeters."),

    threeparttable = TRUE) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "scale_down")
```

The distribution of the diamond depths as shown in @tbl-depth follows a similar
pattern to that of length and width, as the Ideal cut diamonds are once again
the smallest in depth according to most of the summary statistics, and the Fair
cut diamonds are the largest. The Fair cut diamonds are the most variable, and
the Ideal cut diamonds the least variable. There is an outlier maximum in the
Very Good cut diamonds, as their maximum value is far larger than that of all
the other cuts.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-depth
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive Statistics of Diamond Depth by Cut Quality"
#| tbl-pos: H

# Step 3: Make new data frame and select only needed data ----

    filter(z != 0) |>

)
## Step 6: Create clean table ----
diamondsDepth |>

                  "Median", "60%-tile", "80%-tile", "Max", "SAM", "SASD"),
    format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
```

Across @tbl-length, @tbl-width, and @tbl-depth, the trend of fair cut diamonds
being the largest and ideal cut diamonds being the smallest across their
respective dimensions is revealed. Additionally, the trend of fair cut diamonds
having the highest variability and ideal cut diamonds having the lowest
variability is shown, which aligns with the fact that fair cut diamonds have the
smallest frequency, and the ideal cut diamonds have the largest, each by a
sizable margin.

# Big 10 Academic Alliance - Love Data Week

```{r}
#| label: fig-ncaaShooting
#| fig-cap: >-
#|  "2026 NCAA Women's Basketball AP Top 25 Shooting Efficiency 
#|  Landscape by Win Tier"
#| fig-alt: >-
#|  "Two-panel scatter plot of 2026 women’s basketball teams, with team logos
#|  positioned by team and opponent field-goal percentages; elite-tier teams
#|  include several high-shooting, strong-defense teams."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.5

# Step 2: Load Data ----
box_raw <- read.csv(
  file = "team_box.csv",
  header = TRUE,
  sep = ","
)
# Step 3A: Filter out unneeded seasons ----
box_tidy <- box_raw |>
  filter(season == 2026)
# Step 3B: Create Opponent Data Frame ----
opp_box <- box_raw |>
  filter(season == 2026) |>
  select(
    game_id,
    opponent = team_slug,
    opp_fg_pct = field_goal_pct
  )
# Step 3C: Combine to one data frame ----
box_total <- box_tidy |>
  inner_join(opp_box, by = "game_id") |>
  filter(team_slug != opponent)
# Step 4C: Combine into season averages ----
box_averages <- box_total |>
  group_by(team_slug, team_abbreviation, team_logo) |>
  summarize(
    game_count = n(),
    win_pct = round(mean(team_winner, na.rm = TRUE), digits = 2),
    avg_team_fg_pct = round(mean(field_goal_pct, na.rm = TRUE),digits = 2),
    avg_opp_fg_pct = round(mean(opp_fg_pct, na.rm = TRUE),digits = 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
# Step 5: Load Ranking data ----
rankings_raw <- read.csv(
  file = "rankings.csv",
  header = TRUE,
  sep = ","
)
# Step 6A: Wrangle Ranking Data ----
rankings_tidy <- rankings_raw |>
  slice_head( n = 25) |>
  select(current, team_abbreviation)
#Step 6B: Join Data Frames ----
top_box <- box_averages |>
  inner_join(rankings_tidy, by = "team_abbreviation") |>
  filter(game_count >= 30) |>
  select(-team_abbreviation)
# Step 6C: Calculate center lines ----
mean_x <- mean(top_box$avg_team_fg_pct)
mean_y <- mean(top_box$avg_opp_fg_pct)
# Step 7: Facet Data ----
top_box_faceted <- top_box |>
  mutate(
    win_tier = case_when(
      win_pct >= 0.80 ~ "Elite Tier (80%+ Wins)",
      win_pct >= 0.65 ~ "Contender Tier (65%-79% Wins)"
    ),
    win_tier = factor(win_tier, 
        levels = c("Contender Tier (65%-79% Wins)","Elite Tier (80%+ Wins)"))
  )
# Step 8: Create Plot ----
ggplot(
  data = top_box_faceted,
  mapping = aes(
    x = avg_team_fg_pct,
    y = avg_opp_fg_pct
  )) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean_x, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean_y, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_image(
    mapping = aes(
      image = team_logo),
    size = 0.07,
    by = "width",
    use_cache = TRUE) +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  facet_wrap(~win_tier) +
  labs(
    x = "Average Team Season Field Goal %",
    y = "Average Opponent Season Field Goal %",
    title = "NCAA Women's Basketball 2026 Shooting Efficiency Landscape",
    subtitle = 
      "AP Top 25 Teams Final 2026 Season Rankings Faceted by Win Thresholds",
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = mean_x - 3.5, y = mean_y + 4,
           label = "Weak Both Ways", color = "#999999", size = 2.5) +
  annotate("text", x = mean_x + 3.5, y = mean_y + 4,
           label = "Strong Offense & Weak Defense",
           color = "#999999", size = 2.5) +
  annotate("text", x = mean_x - 3, y = mean_y - 4,
           label = "Weak Offense & Strong Defense",
           color = "#999999", size = 2.5) +
  annotate("text", x = mean_x + 2.5, y = mean_y - 4,
           label = "Strong Both Ways", color = "#999999", size = 2.5) +
  theme_bw() +
  annotate(
    "text", 
    x = mean_x, 
    y = min(top_box$avg_opp_fg_pct, na.rm = TRUE), 
    label = paste0("Avg: ", round(mean_x * 1,2), "%"), 
    angle = 90, 
    vjust = -0.75,
    hjust = 1,
    color = "#999999",
    size = 3
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text", 
    x = max(top_box$avg_team_fg_pct, na.rm = TRUE), 
    y = mean_y, 
    label = paste0("Avg: ", round(mean_y * 1,2), "%"), 
    hjust = 1, 
    vjust = -0.75,
    color = "#999999",
    size = 3
  )
```

@fig-ncaaShooting reveals the relationships between three attributes of the top
25 AP ranked NCAA women's basketball teams from the 2026 college season. The
chart plots the relationship between each team's season average field goal
percentage and that of their opponents. The chart is faceted into two
subsections, with the strongest of the teams being on the right. This reveals
that the majority of the best teams by winning percentage were elite in both
scoring efficiency and defensive efficiency. Out of the teams that were above
the average of 46.33% in scoring efficiency, seven out of the nine made it into
the elite tier, showing the importance of efficient offense towards winning
games. A smaller share of teams that were better than the average of 38.35% in
the opponent average field goal percentage attribute made the elite tier at six
out of twelve, showing that for these teams, offense was a better predictor of
winning. Two teams in the elite tier were below average in both attributes,
which reveals that these attributes are not perfect predictors of a team's
success, and that there are other important aspects of basketball beyond those
measured in the chart.

# Monte Carlo Numerical Integration

```{r}
#| label: coordinateGeneration
#| include: false

generateCoords <- function(numPoints, xMin, xMax, yMin, yMax) {
  simData <- tibble(
    x = runif(numPoints, min = xMin, max = xMax),
    y = runif(numPoints, min = yMin, max = yMax)
  )
  
  return(simData)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-monteCarlo
#| fig-cap: >-
#|  "Monte Carlo Numerical Integration Estimates for a Chi-Square
#|   Distribution (df = 5) Across Sample Sizes"
#| fig-subcap: 
#|   - "Sample Size of 10"
#|   - "Sample Size of 100"
#|   - "Sample Size of 1000"
#|   - "Sample Size of 10000"
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   - "Monte Carlo integration graph showing a curve that peaks near x = 3,
#|    with eight magenta “above” points and two green “on/below” points;
#|     estimated numerical integration is 0.64."
#|   - "Scatter plot of 100 points around a curve that peaks near x = 3
#|    and declines toward zero; points are colored red for “above” and green
#|     for “on/below.” Estimated numerical integration: 1.216."
#|   - "Scatter plot of 1,000 Monte Carlo points classified as above or
#|    on/below a black curve; the estimated numerical integration is 0.9952."
#|   - "Monte Carlo scatter plot of 10,000 points, with green points at or
#|    below a peaked black curve and magenta points above; estimated numerical
#|     integration is 1.0147."
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| aria-describedby: monteCarlo2LD
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| fig-pos: H

# Plot 1 ----
set.seed(565)
sim_data <- generateCoords(10, 0, 20, 0, 0.16)
# Step 3: Flag point locations ----
sim_data <- sim_data |>
  mutate(
    curveFunc = dchisq(x, df = 5),
    Flag = ifelse(y <= curveFunc, "on/below", "above")
  )
# Step 4: Calculate numerical integration estimate ----
boxArea = 20 * 0.16
propBelow <- mean(sim_data$Flag == "on/below")
estIntegration <- boxArea * propBelow
# Step 5: Format text for display ----
estLabel <- paste("Est. Numerical Integration = ", round(estIntegration, 4))
# Step 6: Create Plot ----
ggplot(
    data = sim_data,
    mapping = aes(
     x = x,
      y = y
   ) 
  ) +
  geom_point(
    mapping = aes(color = Flag)
  ) +
  stat_function(
   fun = dchisq,
   args = list(df = 5),
   xlim = c(0, 20)
   ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("#BC204B","#99CC00")
  ) +
  labs(
   title = paste("Monte Carlo Integration Example, n =", nrow(sim_data)),
    subtitle = estLabel,
   x = "x",
   y = "y",
   color = "Flag"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

# Plot 2 ----
set.seed(565)
sim_data <- generateCoords(100, 0, 20, 0, 0.16)
# Step 3: Flag point locations ----
sim_data <- sim_data |>
  mutate(
    curveFunc = dchisq(x, df = 5),
    Flag = ifelse(y <= curveFunc, "on/below", "above")
  )
# Step 4: Calculate numerical integration estimate ----
boxArea = 20 * 0.16
propBelow <- mean(sim_data$Flag == "on/below")
estIntegration <- boxArea * propBelow
# Step 5: Format text for display ----
estLabel <- paste("Est. Numerical Integration = ", round(estIntegration, 4))
# Step 6: Create Plot ----
ggplot(
    data = sim_data,
    mapping = aes(

      y = y
   ) 
  ) +
  geom_point(
    mapping = aes(color = Flag)
  ) +

   ) +

    subtitle = estLabel,
   x = "x",

    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

#Plot 3 ----
set.seed(565)
sim_data <- generateCoords(1000, 0, 20, 0, 0.16)
# Step 3: Flag point locations ----
sim_data <- sim_data |>
  mutate(
    curveFunc = dchisq(x, df = 5),

# Step 4: Calculate numerical integration estimate ----

```

@fig-monteCarlo reveals information about Monte Carlo simulations, primarily how
simulations work, and the resulting numerical integration based off of them. It
is shown that Monte Carlo simulation is the process of which a numerical
integration is estimated by using points and flagging them based on whether they
fit within a function. The small multiple displays that as the sample size of
points increases in size, the variability of the Monte Carlo test decreases,
leading to a more accurate answer with more points. I estimate the exact answer
to the numerical integration is 1, as in each plot, as the sample size
increases, the estimated numerical integration gets closer and closer to one,
starting at being 0.36 away with 10 points as seen in @fig-monteCarlo-1, to
0.0147 away with a sample size of 10,000 as seen in @fig-monteCarlo-4. The small
multiple supports this conclusion by not only stating the estimated numerical
integration for each plot, but also by displaying the results visually, with
each subsequent plot becoming more dense, and therefore less variable. The small
multiple would help somebody come to this conclusion by not only giving number
figures for the estimates, but also by showing a visualization of what is
actually being done to estimate the value of the numerical integration.

# Planning and Prompting GenAI Tools

In this section, I will compare and contrast the results of a AI-generated data
visualization created using a specific human-created plan and an AI-generated
visualization created using a generic prompt.

## Plan {#sec-Plan}

The First step of this section is to create a plan that I will give to an AI for
it to attempt to wrangle the original data file and create a data visualization
for it.

### Goals & Sub-Goals

The goal of this task is to analyze the development of calcium levels in each
group over the three-year span using a data visualization.

**Sub-Goals:**

1.  Decide how to wrangle the data from its original formatting.
2.  Wrangle the data into a clean format for creating the visualization.
3.  Decide what type of data visualization would best suit the analysis.
4.  Create the data visualization and customize Elementary Perceptual Tasks
    (EPTs).

### Nouns & Verbs

**Nouns:**

- **Importing and Loading:** `RStudio`, `tidyverse`
- **Data Frames:** `calcium_raw`, `calcium_Tidy`
- **Original Columns:** `y0`, `y1`, `y2`, `y3`, `y0.1`, `y1.1`, `y2.1`, `y3.1`
- **Tidy Columns:** `raw_Name`, `year`, `group`, `calcium_Level`
- **Other:** `calcium.csv`, `","`, `"y"`, `"."`, `align_start`, `control`,
  `treatment`, `digits`, `data`
- **Values:** `3`, `1.25`, `2.5`
- **Colors:** `#1E407C`, `#BC204B`, `PSU palette`
- **Plot-Related:** `x`, `y`, `color`, `linewidth`, `size`, `legend.position`,
  `title`, `subtitle`

**Verbs:**

- **Data & Package Importing:** `library()`, `read.csv()`
- **Summarizing:** `summarise()`, `across()`, `mean()`, `round()`,
  `starts_with()`
- **Tidying:** `pivot_longer()`, `everything()`, `separate_wider_delim()`,
  `mutate()`, `as.numeric()`, `str_remove()`, `ifelse()`, `is.na()`
- **Visualization:** `ggplot()`, `aes()`, `geom_line()`, `geom_point()`, `c()`,
  `labs()`, `theme_bw()`, `theme()`, `scale_color_manual()`

### Coding Plan

1.  Open RStudio and load `tidyverse` using `library()`.
2.  Use `read.csv()` to import `"calcium.csv"`, saving it into the new data
    frame `calcium_raw`.
    - Since it is a CSV file, set `sep` to `","`.
3.  Use `summarise()` to compute the mean of all yearly measurements for the new
    data frame `calcium_Tidy`.
    - Within `summarise()`, use `across()` and `starts_with("y")` to cover all
      original columns (`y0`, `y1`, `y2`, `y3`, `y0.1`, `y1.1`, `y2.1`, `y3.1`).
    - Set `digits` within `round()` to `3` so the new values display three
      decimal places.
4.  Use `pivot_longer()` to reshape the data frame into a long format.
    - Use `everything()` to apply the pivot to all columns.
    - Send the column names to the new column `raw_Name`.
    - Send the values to the new column `calcium_Level`.
5.  Use `separate_wider_delim()` to split the `raw_Name` column.
    - Set `delim` to `"."`, as this distinguishes between control and treatment
      data.
    - Use `c()` to set the names of the new columns to `year` and `group`.
    - Set `too_few = "align_start"` to prevent errors from missing suffixes on
      the control columns.
6.  Use `mutate()` to tidy the new columns.
    - Use `str_remove()` on `year` to remove the `"y"` prefix.
    - Use `as.numeric()` to convert `year` into numerical values.
    - Use `ifelse()` and `is.na()` on `group` to assign `"Control"` and
      `"Treatment"` labels.
7.  Create the data visualization.
    - Use `ggplot()` with `data` set to `calcium_Tidy`.
    - Set `mapping` using `aes()`, mapping `x` to `year`, `y` to
      `calcium_Level`, and `color` to `group`.
    - Use `geom_line()` to draw the lines, setting `linewidth` to `1.25`.
    - Use `geom_point()` to plot the data points, setting `size` to `2.5`.
    - Use `scale_color_manual()` with `c()` to set the line colors to `#1E407C`
      and `#BC204B` from a PSU palette.
    - Use `labs()` to set the labels for the title, legend color, x-axis,
      y-axis, subtitle, and alt text.
    - Use `theme_bw()` to apply a clean background theme.
    - Use `theme()` and set `legend.position = "bottom"` to move the legend
      below the plot.

## ChatGPT-generated Plan-Informed Visualization vs. ChatGPT-generated Visualization Made With Generic Prompt

In order to create a comparison between a data visualization created based on a
human-made plan and that of a generic AI prompt, I created the plan seen above,
and gave it to ChatGPT for it to follow, as well as received a generic ChatGPT
response and the visualization that was included with it.

## Plan-Informed AI Data Visualization

```{r}
#| label: fig-informedCalcium
#| fig-cap: "Plan-Informed AI Calcium Study Analysis Plot"
#| fig-alt: >- 
#|  "Line graph of mean calcium levels for control and treatment groups across
#|   Years 0–3; both groups drop sharply by Year 3."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4

# Load packages
library(tidyverse)

# Import the original data
calcium_raw <- read.csv("calcium.csv", sep = ",")

# Calculate the mean for each year and group, rounded to three decimals
calcium_Tidy <- calcium_raw %>%
  summarise(
    across(
      starts_with("y"),
      ~ round(mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE), digits = 3)
    )
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "raw_Name",
    values_to = "calcium_Level"
  ) %>%
  separate_wider_delim(
    raw_Name,
    delim = ".",
    names = c("year", "group"),
    too_few = "align_start"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    year = as.numeric(str_remove(year, "y")),
    group = ifelse(is.na(group), "Control", "Treatment")
  )

# Create the visualization
calcium_Plot <- ggplot(
  data = calcium_Tidy,
  mapping = aes(x = year, y = calcium_Level, color = group)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.25) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Control" = "#1E407C", "Treatment" = "#BC204B")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean Calcium Levels Over Three Years",
    subtitle = "Comparison of the control and treatment groups",
    color = "Group",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean Calcium Level",
    alt = "Line graph comparing mean calcium levels in the control
    and treatment groups from year 0 through year 3."
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

# Display the plot
calcium_Plot
```

One important note: The script calculates the means before pivoting because the
goal is to compare the average calcium levels of the two groups across the four
years.

## Human-made plot

```{r}
#| label: fig-humanCalcium
#| fig-cap: "Human-coded Calcium Study Analysis Plot"
#| fig-alt: >- 
#|  "Line graph of mean calcium levels for control and 
#|  treatment groups from Years 0–3; both drop sharply at Year 3."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
calcium_Raw <- read.csv(
  file = "calcium.csv",
  header = TRUE,
  sep = ","
)
# Step 3: Wrangle Data ----
calcium_Tidy <- calcium_Raw |>
  summarise(
    across(
      .cols = starts_with("y"),
      .fns = ~ round(mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE), digits = 3)
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "raw_Name",
    values_to = "calcium_Level"
  ) |>
  separate_wider_delim(
    cols = raw_Name,
    delim = ".",
    names = c("year", "group"),
    too_few = "align_start"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    year = as.numeric(str_remove(year, "y")),
    group = ifelse(is.na(group), "Control", "Treatment")
  )
## Create Line Graph of Calcium Levels ----
ggplot(
  data = calcium_Tidy,
  mapping = aes(
    x = year,
    y = calcium_Level,
    color = group
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.25) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_manual( 
    values = c("#1E407C", "#BC204B")) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean Calcium Levels in Women Over a Three-Year Study",
    subtitle = "Comparing Control vs. Special Diet and Exercise
    Treatment Groups (Years 0–3)",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean Calcium Level",
    color = "Condition",
    alt = "Line graph of mean calcium levels for control and treatment
    groups from Years 0–3; both drop sharply at Year 3."
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
```

## Comparison

Contrasting the three data visualization displays the importance of human
analytic reasoning and planning. @fig-informedCalcium was generated using a plan
that was created with an understanding of the context of the study, which mean
the AI was able to properly wrangle the data into a format that was capable of
highlighting the results of the study. It has many features that @fig-AICalcium
does not, including a proper title and subtitle, colors, a legend, and separated
glyphs for the two groups of the experiment. In contrast, with a generic prompt,
ChatGPT only knew the numbers, and not the situation, leading to it creating a
chart that doesn't depict the intention of the study. Because of how the
original data file was formatted, the AI combined both experimental groups onto
a single x-axis rather than separating them for comparison. The generic-prompted
chart misrepresents the structure of the experiment, while the plan-informed
chart is able to accurately convey the data and the message it supports. There
are few differences between the human-made chart, @fig-humanCalcium, and
@fig-informedCalcium, due to the precision of the plan, they are almost
identical apart from differences in the title and subtitle, and the grid lines.
This shows that even with a very precise plan, the human mind's ability to truly
comprehend context gives it an advantage over generative AI.

# Reflection

I have learned a great amount of information about the world of R and
statistical analysis during this semester. The main topics which I have found
the most important are learning the principles of data and open science,
learning how to wrangle data, learning how to create tables and data
visualizations, learning what makes a strong data visualization, learning how to
make plans, and learning how to use quarto markdown. I have learned that the key
behind strong statistical analysis and a healthy community is responsibility,
respect, and making things easily accessible. There are many principles behind
how statistics should be handled, and I've learned that different situations
have their different rules. For example, it is a key principle that statistical
analysis should not be used to discriminate or harm marginalized communities,
and it is important that all authors of a project be properly credited. I've
learned that one of the first steps to any analysis is wrangling data, which was
key in how I created @fig-humanCalcium. Often times data will be in a format
that isn't suitable for analysis, so a statistician must use their skills to
work the data into a format that they can have for further use, such as making a
data visualization. @fig-monteCarlo demonstrates how there are many aspects that
go into creating data visualizations, from elementary perceptual tasks, to
different types of displays, to even things like faceting. It is up to the
statistician to decide what a data visualization should look like, and they must
consider their audience, as well as the needs of the differently-abled. Data
visualizations are meant to convey a message that one could miss if they were to
just look at the data itself. I've learned that certain EPTs are easier for the
general public to understand, like direction, while some like shading are more
difficult, which factors into the statistician's decisions. I would say that
making data visualizations is my favorite part of statistics, I find them very
enjoyable to create, and I think making them is one of my best strengths as a
statistician. I've learned through experience that planning is a critical part
of every process, which can be seen in @sec-Plan, as well as in the differences
between @Fig-informedCalcium and @Fig-AICalcium. Making a plan is an important
step for staying grounded and on task. I think that making plans is something
that I can improve on, as I tend to channel my effort into the other processes
rather than focusing on it initially, which is something I should try to change.
Quarto markdown is a new concept, but I understand that it is the bridge between
code and a proper report, so it is something that I need to practice and focus
on for the future.
